posts.author: RCXGaming
posts.body:
I have a lot of different "complex" moments because the amount of detail I put in is nightmarish, but my favorite planned one is something I'd like to call the "Use More Than Just Normal Attack" moment.
Aight, so you're put up against three peculiar enemies: A zombie priestess and two ghouls.
The priestess is armed with something called Tyrant Aura, which makes it so any damage she takes is filtered to her allies instead. Her ghouls both have passives called "Reflex" which makes it so any normal attack thrown their way is automatically dodged. Makes you think "Oh, wait, passive abilities are more than just stat boosts?"
Every fourth turn, Ms. Zombie Priestess will heal her entire party with Unholy Embrace to patch up any partial damage you did to the ghouls. It teaches you about patterns and that you can't just swing blindly to succeed, you have to use your skills with a purpose. Do you strike her to hit everyone, or do you get rid of the ghouls piece-by-piece?
Design like this is also iterated upon as the game goes on - it's not just contained here.

posts.author: Robro33
posts.body:
Not sure if it counts as the most complex, but its one of my favorites.
A boss/class has the the ability to place a state called Timeslip on a battler that perfectly records them as they were when it was placed, and then reverts them back to as they were when it expires.
I ended up taking a few pages out of FFXIV Gaia's playbook with "Spell in Waiting" for the boss. The boss regularly places delayed spells on characters as states that go off when the state expires, and then can choose for some the effects trigger a second time a few turns later by applying Timeslip to the character just before spell in waiting expires
The class is limited to only being able to use it on party members (atleast until i figure out how exactly i want it to interact with troop events when on enemies), but it enables tons of shenanigans revolving around cooldowns, class resources, and current equipment because you can prepare a burst, apply the state, spend the burst, then yoink the quarter back out the vending machine and burst again.
For the player, the skill has no cooldown or mp cost, but the class's mechanic is that it builds up and spends up your file's playtime with its skills as a shared partywide resource.

posts.author: ISC
posts.body:
Where do I start? Okay, with the simplest one.
Sturdust:
A mechanic that wasn’t too complex but I enjoyed creating involved linking base parameters (attack, defense, etc.) with Ex and Sp parameters so they could receive bonuses. For example, for every point in agility, you would gain a percentage bonus on physical evasion. Or, your max HP would increase for every point in physical defense. I made sure to correlate one or more Ex and Sp parameters to each base parameter.
The Dice Keeper:
A prototype where the battle system is controlled by dice rolls, much like *Hero Quest* (a 90s board game). The special feature was the ability to customize the faces of the dice, changing individual sides. Each special side would trigger effects like lightning, fire, or poison.
The Demon's Holiday:
A satirical and absurd game where you can customize different aspects such as:
- Guard Command: Choose a bonus effect in addition to the standard guard command.
- Forge: Create your ideal equipment, choosing attack, defense, etc.
In this prototype, I also included a rock-paper-scissors minigame where the opponent uses a specific strategy, so there’s a small AI.
Feud:
A management system for a feudal estate, inspired by board games like Stone Age. It uses a deck of random but non-repeating event cards, similar to Stronghold.
On an experimental level, I’ve added many different skills, some crazy, some completely useless .

posts.author: Maliki79
posts.body:
So, I guess the most complex part of my game would be the battle system in general.
The complexity comes from how the different pieces themselves come together.
I have a basic combo system that counts consecutive hits from the player party.
Each hit raises the damage of following attacks.
And enemies not only break the combo when they hit, but begin building their own counter.
(Misses and evades - which I "fixed" in my game) do NOT reset the counter, so high evade PCs and lot hit states are good strategies to build high combo counts.
PCs level up via point spending ala Dark Souls.  Skills are also purchasable with those same points AND require items.  And speaking of items...
Enemies can have multiple items stolen in a battle!
Most enemies have at least 2 items that can be stolen.  And some of those are from VERY powerful enemies where the strategy is basically to steal as much as you can as fast as you can and literally run away afterwards.
Drops are determined by how you beat an enemy.
So the basic one in my game is the Oneshot, which you have to kill an enemy in one hit.
There are others depending on the enemy.
Like killing a slime while it has a "Burn" makes it drop Charred Slime, which COULD be a quest item.
Next is stat buildup.
So most of the percentage based states I have have a buildup system.
So, for example, Poison.
At the end of an action, the poisoned target will take a little damage.
but if the buildup is say 10%, they might only take 10% hp loss.
If it goes up to 100%, you can potentially OTK even a boss!
I have defenses too counter act this, so it's not too easily exploited.
Then there's the party composition.
Any party member can have any skill.
So, if you need all members tossing flame spells, do it!
If they need to Use swords to pile on combo after combo, go for it!
If they need to steal from a murderous fish before it nukes them, it's gravy!
But the player needs to figure out when and how top pull it all off.
It's a lot, and I want to make it even more intricate, but I have to build on these aspects slowly.

posts.author: Villhelm
posts.body:
I wouldn't say this one's the most mechanically complex in my game, but it is overly complex.
My swashbuckler / alchemist Genevieve has a really complicated basic attack called Lunge.
On its own its a basic single hit attack.
It can be empowered with envenoms that add poison, paralysis, or anti-heal status effects that have a number of doses that scale with her Alchemy skill count.
It can also be empowered with arcanums which can allow her to steal buffs from the enemy, or ignore armor, or turn it into a triple attack (this also changes the animation colour of the hits).
It is also affected by which stance she's in. Either she is using her offhand dagger defensively, on which case she can get crit chance bonuses on Lunge after a successful parry/riposte, or she dual wields the dagger and gets an extra attack.
It also is affected by conditional follow up fencing skills. If any hit of Lunge misses, she gets a guaranteed hit Remise that does reduced damage. If any hit of Lunge critically hits, she gets an execute-style Coup de Grace attack for even more bonus damage.
So, for example at end game, if she prepares the Poison envenom and the Quick arcanum on her blades (which are QTEs in their own right) and successfully parry/ripostes an opponent, her next Lunge basic attack would:
Be a guaranteed critical hit.
Strike three times.
Trigger a fourth Coup de Grace attack.
Apply 4 doses of poison assuming all attacks hit.
The action sequence for her basic attack is about 150 lines of code...

The gimmick is that the the different spells in waiting create different immediate goals for each character. The interaction with Timeslip is that depending on when she uses it, it can either end up with the spell being repeated,
or
the duration being extended while essentially erasing their individual mechanics during the time the slip is active. She'll only ever timeslip someone with a spell in waiting, but the approach is random.
Spoiler:
kinda rambly
Unlike alot of other boss negative state mechanics, spells in waiting do not persist on death and can have their durations extended/shortened through some class skills and effects, BUT TImeslip does persist, its duration cannot be changed, and will revive someone at the end of it if they died during it
She has a total of 6 spells in waiting.
two are aoes:
the first is moderate physical party damage with a DEF debuff. its severity is based on the number of hits that party member has taken during its duration.
the second is a magical ice damage that reduces the ice resistance of any target that it deals a minimum amount of damage to based on her stats
the third is an ST ice skill that cannot miss under most circumstances and bypasses a moderate portion of DEF. secondarily, its a drain that she uses to restore bits of her HP and her remaining "time". but like the ice aoe, the secondary effects only happen if a damage minimum was met
the fourth when placed on a target starts a counter of 8. it expires in 5 turns and the counter is reduced by 1 whenever the target deals an instance of damage to the boss. when the spell in waiting goes off, all of the boss's cooldowns for their normal skills are reduced by the number of the remaining counter
the 5th records the statuses and debuffs she herself applies to the effected battler during its duration alongside all the net damage/healing over time they had from any source in that time. at the end, it applies each of them to one random party member, Timeslip being exempt
The last one records any healing/buffs the battler applies to anyone, and then on expiration: transfers the buffs from the party member to the boss, and gives the boss a heal over time equal to the total healing dealt for a few turns
When she assigns them, each living party member gets one at random with a semi-randomized duration, but with a few rules.
- No repeats
- the first and the second are mutually exclusive in a set
- the 5th can only be assigned if the 1st was chosen, trending towards expiring later
- the 6th can only be assigned if the 2nd was chosen, trending towards expiring sooner
last bit i think is important is that if at any time a spell in waiting was removed because the target died, the effect doesnt happen. However, she gains a temporary stacking, ramping, multiplicative damage increase. its a couple turns and starts low, but if you repeatedly sac people or allow them to die in order to clear consecutive spells in waiting, it becomes a problem (or challenge if the player wishes to see it that way. theres enough tools to cobble a plan around it together if class comps are played around with)

posts.author: Lord Vectra
posts.body:
The most complex system I made so far is my level up system for my current project.
You have traits which are your roleplay stats (persuasion, might, lockpickin etc).
You have your regular stats (HP, STR, etc)
Then you have masteries which are essentially psuedo-skill trees (longblade, shortblade, fire, water).
You get 1 Trait point per 2 levels. You get 3 stat points per level. 10 mastery points per level.
Your stats start at 20. Your traits start at 0. All your masteries start at 15.
Your traits also increases by 1 per 4pts over 20 its respective stat is (i.e. A 40 Str means your might is a minimum of 5).
For masteries, each one has 4 tiers (think of it like apprentice, journeyman, expert, and master as seen in Elder Scrolls). Each Tier has 4 skills each. The minimum Mastery Level to unlock a tier is 25, 50, 75, and 100 respectively. Then you have learning points. The amount of learning points you have in each mastery is equal to their mastery levels. The Learning Costs of spells are based on their tier and are 10, 20, 30, and 40 respectively.
You can't switch out skills whenever you please and same with respecs.
Skills that you select to learn will appear blue on the screen (visual feedback that you have learned it). Skills that you learn *outside* of the leveling system (aka the add skill event command) appear gold. Life has a spell called "Heal." If you select it as a skill, it'll be blue. If you learn it outside of this method, it will appear gold and will not count against you on learning points. It will also refund you on learning points and allow you to switch it out for something else.
Probably the most ambitious system I have made.

Hm, most of my complex pieces have to do with passives in my game. Things like:
-MC has a perma-kill passive, where anything he kills can't be revived. It wasn't 'complex' to implement (it's...one line in a passive state lol) but it certainly is a fun mechanic to play around with
-Both the passives for my healer are pretty great, if I do so say myself. His innate passive generates a shield on himself every other turn in combat. If he's taken damage, it's based on his Max HP, but if he hasn't, it's a good chunk of his current HP. His learnable passive auto-cleanses up to 2 harmful states from all (alive! some states bypass death) allies every turn in combat, and restores 8% of their Max HP if the effect procs
-Final boss gets an auto-res passive. Yup. You read that right. The final boss automatically self-revives.
There's also a puzzle I'm pretty proud of
It's like the FFX sphere puzzles; you take a coloured sphere, can only hold one at a time, and have to put it in the right pillar. Need 5 correct spheres in correct places. The answers are in your menu. But, you can also use the audio cues instead!
Uh, a massive cutscene I did was super fun. It's....the joke chase scene where everyone runs down a hallway, going in a door and coming out a completely different one. It's like that! Where the chaser becomes the chasee and it's just general chaos. I can never watch that cutscene with a straight face; I always end up on the floor laughing.
Oh! And one last thing that I absolutely adore...a skill. Specifically, a special skill of the final boss. It gets cast automatically and is instant-cast upon a certain condition in battle. It hits everything alive. Removes all states - good and bad - from everything. Damages your party for 5% MHP + 2% per time cast. Heals her for 5% MHP + 1% per time cast. It has no cast limit - so yes, proc the condition enough times, and it could in theory deal all your MHP in one go.
It was a pain in the rear to make and get working properly, given it's supposed to go off the second the condition is met, regardless of whose turn it is. But it works beautifully, and I love it.
I have some more, but, uh, I'm trying to avoid going on long-winded rants about stuff

posts.author: freakytapir
posts.body:
I made a three action turn system where each player character gets 3 action points a turn, and can spend them however he likes between 2, 1 or 0 point actions.
So a Spell would be a 2 point action, a basic attack would be a 1 action thing, with the addition of a harsh damage debuff if you spam just spam attack three times. (So basically full damage, half and a quarter damage if you just spam attack three times, for 1.75 the damage of a single attack in total, incentivising you to find a use for that third action).
This works wonders for caster melee hybrids as spells are not attacks, so it is viable for a warpriest to smack someone and cast a cure spell in the same turn, without having to resort to a cludge with "Combined skills" that do both.
Or for a spellblade to cast haste and smack a guy up the head in one turn. or the fighter to smack someone, quaff a potion he has ready, and raise a shield.
It also gives me another knob to turn in the power of an ability. More powerful abilities just take more actions. Or thing like double attack give you two attacks for two actions but the penalty doesn't kick in until both attacks are made (Making your 1.5*damage 2 attacks 2.0*damage at once).
I mean, as usual I overcomplicated it, but eventually it just tooks some states, and common events, a couple of Yanfly plugins and it works like a charm. (and adapting Olivia's Boost point system to serve as an action remaining counter but that is aesthetics and has no gameplay effect).
Or in the production side of things, read my class and enemy stats as a CSV into an external program (Rstudio) and do widespread analisys and wholesale editing of stats in one easy go and overwrite the game stats in one fell swoop. Only took 2 plug-ins (one to make enemies have classes and another one for class parameters to be stored as a CSV file)

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I'm not sure if you would classify this as "mechanically complex".
Inn Event System
On its surface, this works like the Dragon Age Origins "Campsite".  You get to talk to your party members here, occasionally make a choice, sometimes pick up a Quest, and generally just get Characterization/Lore of the world.
How it works in practice is that there are a series of "event flags" that can trigger new stuff, as well as a "pick something random" portion.  When the player selects "stay at Inn" and it fades to black, the system rolls two different variables.  The first variable is for "new events".  The second variable is for "nothing new".
There's probably a lot better way to run this, but here's how it works:
I have 5 variables store information to prevent "repeats" of "events" at the Inn.
Variable 1 (0+Roll Between X and Y number, called New Event)
Variable 2 (If Variable 4 = Z, roll between A and B number, called No New Event)
Variable 3 (tracks amount of rolls made for Variable 1, to prevent skipping events or duplicating them, called Event Control)
Variable 4 (tracks amount of total "points" across Variable 1 rolls.  Called Event Set)
Variable 5 (tracks where the player is in the game, sets a Tier of events)
So, the player stays at the Inn, and they're in the beginning of the game.  They would normally have 0 events to view unless they got a second party member.  Once they have a second party member, they start rolling for "available events" that I control with "If/Then" branches.  If the player hasn't seen/done the relevent thing, it can't be rolled and it defaults to the "No New Stuff" variable to choose the scene.  If something can be rolled from the Event side, the other variables will track what is rolled to keep things from coming up twice.
So, if you're in Tier 1 of events (Variable 5 = 1) you will roll on the 1-3 Event Table (Variable 1 makes a roll between 1-3).  If it lands on 3, Variable 3 will go up by 1 and Variable 4 will add 3 to its total.  If the player had previously seen Event 1 and 2, Variable 3 will be 2, and Variable 4 will be 3... but since Variable 3 is 2, the game can only roll the 3.
This is heavily simplified, by the way.  There's a lot of "If/then" in here checking for things (If Variable 3 is 2, check if Variable 4 is 1, 2, or 3, roll between or select other event, etcetera).
When a new "Tier" is reached, variables are reset back to 0 to do it all again.
I was hoping to craft a system that would do this:
1.  Give the player something new to see each time they stay the the Inn.
2.  Prioritize events the player has not seen over everything else.
3.  Randomize the events so different playstyles might see things at different times.
It's likely very overly complicated, but it does what I want... mostly.  There's also a "variable" for tracking how many party members there are for moving Tiers up and which party members there are, since some events can't trigger if the correct people aren't there...
Anyway, the game will "remember the choices" each character has made, it will remember conversations that have been had, and it will basically make sure you don't see the "important" events more than once.  The characters even "change positions in the room" based on the event rolled.  Sometimes they are talking to each other and you can listen in.  Sometimes, they talk directly to you.  Sometimes, they might even be "absent" from the room to talk to because they're doing something else.
Heck, I even have a small thing in there where the characters "gravitate toward their favorites" after a while (and maybe even after some choices are made).  The biggest example of this is just my "Magic Knight", who will gravitate toward one of three characters depending on how you've treated him and whether you've convinced him (or the three people) of certain values.  Only one of these people is someone he can romance, too.  Yep, that's right, you can help your bud actually romance someone instead of being forever single.  Okay, maybe that's not so cool or unique.
But, it so far runs "seemlessly" as it is with the 5 variables and about a dozen triggers in place (for 3 characters).  I expect to run into problems later with it since it's sort of complex under the hood.

posts.author: Iron_Brew
posts.body:
I gotta say, something I'm really proud of is my dungeon design. I know that these may not fall into "mechanical complexity", but some of the ways I've executed RPG staples are things I'm geniuinely proud of. So it's not really so much about mechanical complexity as it is about tricking the player into thinking complex designs are way simpler than they actually are, and
tricking them into
having fun.
Let's look at this (my latest) dungeon, for example:
It's an unassuming little building with a slime motif on the front.
There's a little moving box puzzle next to it, foreshadowing and tutorialising the mechanics within, allowing you to climb to the roof and get free goodies.
It's a simple gimmick "box push and switch" dungeon where you need to depress four switches to release four locks to get to the boss. Fine, nothing special, right?
Well, there's block pushing puzzles that need to be done to create bridges for the player to walk on, which requires thinking on the Z-Axis in order to get this done. Still nothing terribly clever, right?
The thing I'm proud of here is in the design and implementation of each room and how they build on each other and feed into the dungeon as a whole.
When you enter the dungeon there's a map on the wall you can interact with which flat out tells you where the locks and keys are:
Dead simple, sets the player's expectations clearly, and says 'here's the finite goal for getting through this thing'. They know they came from the South and had to walk to get to the map so that orientates them on the map already, which does the job of having a minimap without actually having the player stop thinking for themselves.
The nearest key to the map is in the bottom left, so most players will go for that - and if they don't, it's no big deal, nothing in here is super groundbreaking.
The puzzle is similar to the one outside, and is set up ins uch a way that you can only move the box onto the button to complete the puzzle once you push the two boxes into the alcoves to complete the bridge. Fine.
Also as an aside one of the boxes starts pressed up against a wall, informing you of the implied possibility of failing a puzzle room by not being able to push a box from a direction, but also tutorialising that you can sometimes get these free by pushing them to a place where that direction is available no big deal
.
What I'm proud of here is that this is all done in eventing, without a single line of script or plugin support. Either box works in either alcove, and because of the layout of the room you can only complete the room after putting both boxes in the alcoves.
Like, if you put the "wrong" box into an alcove it swaps places with the right box and the player never knows:
And the box tops are tied to the relevant box bodies like this:
And when boxes enter their alcove they are swapped with events using the tileset which are marked as walkable so the player can use them like floor:
It's so
simple
but it works so well, and the rest of the dungeon is other variations on this theme.
Using camera scrolls and layout tricks (you can see every puzzle from the corridor next to it, and you can see the goal from 3/4 of the relevant rooms) the player always knows exactly where they are, and how far through the dungeon they are.
People always need to consider sightlines and conveyance in their content design, and I wanted to post this because this dungeon goes from "push a single box a single space to reach the roof" to four equally taxing puzzles around that same simple concept, all culmianting in a battle with an evil Slime King. The player doesn't realise it, because for them it's just four fun simple puzzles executed in a way that induces minimal friction, but out here I'm cackling because I've tricked them into moving boxes and actually enjoying it.
In a dungeon shaped like a slime.
Anyway. I wanted to show this off. Cheers, all.
Edit:
We're allowed a little box-move jumpscare, sometimes.
As a treat.
